# RAG vs. Fine-Tuning vs. Long-Context Prompting for Domain-Specific QA

> **Research question:** Compare the effectiveness of RAG, fine-tuning, and long-context prompting for domain-specific question answering. Use recent academic papers and credible technical sources. Identify evidence, limitations, benchmarks, and practical recommendations.

## Executive Summary

Retrieval-augmented generation achieved the highest exact-match accuracy, 71.4% on average, compared with 64.2% for fine-tuning and 66.8% for long-context prompting [1]. The advantage of retrieval was largest on questions about facts updated after the model’s training cutoff, where RAG scored 68.0% exact match versus 31.5% for fine-tuning [1]. Fine-tuning used 40,000 question-answer pairs generated from the same knowledge base [1]. Fine-tuning on domain data reduced performance on a general-knowledge benchmark by 3.1 points, consistent with partial catastrophic forgetting [2]. Long-context prompting matched retrieval when the relevant passage appeared in the first 10% of the context window but fell 13 points behind retrieval when the passage appeared in the middle of the context [1].

**Key recommendations**
- Use retrieval-augmented generation when answers depend on a large or frequently changing knowledge base [5].
- Use fine-tuning to teach consistent output format, tone and domain terminology rather than to add new facts [5].
- Reserve long-context prompting for small document sets, keeping the most relevant material at the beginning of the context [1].
- Monitor retrieval quality continuously, because retrieval failures dominate answer errors [5].

## Accuracy of Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-augmented generation achieved the highest exact-match accuracy, 71.4% on average, compared with 64.2% for fine-tuning and 66.8% for long-context prompting [1]. Increasing chunk size from 256 to 1,024 tokens improved faithfulness on long-form answers by 5 points but reduced precision on factoid questions by 4 points [3]. Across five deployments, retrieval-augmented systems cost between $0.40 and $1.10 per 1,000 queries for retrieval infrastructure in addition to model inference [4].

## Fine-Tuning and Knowledge Injection

Fine-tuning on domain data reduced performance on a general-knowledge benchmark by 3.1 points, consistent with partial catastrophic forgetting [2]. Fine-tuning required an up-front training cost and periodic retraining; teams retrained every 4 to 8 weeks to keep knowledge current [4]. Use fine-tuning to teach a model a consistent output format, tone or task-specific behavior; fine-tuning is not a reliable way to add new factual knowledge [5]. In contrast, one blog source claims that fine-tuning makes the model really learn the domain knowledge, so you never need to update an index [6].

## Long-Context Prompting and Position Effects

Long-context prompting matched retrieval when the relevant passage appeared in the first 10% of the context window but fell 13 points behind retrieval when the passage appeared in the middle of the context [1]. Accuracy was 81% when the relevant passage was at the beginning of the context and 58% when it was in the middle, recovering to 74% when it was at the end [7]. Long-context prompting with 100,000-token prompts was the most expensive option, costing 10 to 20 times more per query than retrieval with 8,000-token prompts [4].

## Cost, Latency and Operations

The advantage of retrieval was largest on questions about facts updated after the model’s training cutoff, where RAG scored 68.0% exact match versus 31.5% for fine-tuning [1]. Processing a 100K-token context cost roughly 12 times more per query than a retrieval pipeline that supplied 8K tokens [7]. Retrieval pipelines require monitoring of retrieval quality, because a retrieval failure rate above 15% typically dominates answer errors [5].

## Practical Guidance

Fine-tuning used 40,000 question-answer pairs generated from the same knowledge base [1]. The report recommends retrieval for large, changing corpora and fine-tuning for stable, behavior-focused tasks [4]. Use retrieval-augmented generation when answers depend on a large or frequently changing knowledge base, because the index can be updated without retraining the model [5].

## Recommendations

- Use retrieval-augmented generation when answers depend on a large or frequently changing knowledge base [5].
- Use fine-tuning to teach consistent output format, tone and domain terminology rather than to add new facts [5].
- Reserve long-context prompting for small document sets, keeping the most relevant material at the beginning of the context [1].
- Monitor retrieval quality continuously, because retrieval failures dominate answer errors [5].

Evidence…) is inconsistent with 'Fine-tuning makes the model really learn the domain knowledge, so you never need to update an index.' ([Synthetic] Why Fine-Tuning Beats RAG Every Time). [2][6]
